selection_policy: Every record must be absent from the main super-2.0 dataset under its canonical spelling, documented Romanized variants, or exact source-script form.

Batch b2 is authenticity-first: candidates were chosen for well-attested lexical or scriptural bases and documented naming usage; demand signals were collected secondarily and are kept scope-specific. Three initial candidates (Samad, Hunayn, Mubashir) were rejected when the collision audit found their script forms already present in the dataset under other spellings (Samat, Haneen/Hanin, Mubasher).
Meanings are checked against lexical, scriptural, or language references; name-site claims are not treated as dictionaries.
Quranic verse references are cited by chapter:verse and checked against the Quran text; a word's occurrence in a verse does not establish a personal-name claim.

Popularity evidence is stored with its source, place, year, metric, and limitation; unlike measures are never combined into a global score, and every record keeps popularity.score null. Site-internal directory ranks are labelled as such and are not population data.
Optional numerology, lucky attributes, personality claims, and invented stories are suppressed. Non-English glosses are editorial drafts requiring native review.

names.name: Ilyasa
names.morphology: Qur'anic Arabic proper name of a prophet; the underlying name is the Hebrew Ĕlîšāʿ (Elisha), so no Arabic triliteral root is asserted.
names.short_meaning: Al-Yasa (Elisha); a prophet named in the Qur'an.
names.primary_meaning: Ilyasa (al-yasaʿ) is the Qur'anic Arabic form of the prophet name Elisha, named in the Qur'an among the prophets of the Israelite line; the record asserts the scriptural reference, not any additional biography.
names.literal_meaning: The form الْيَسَع occurs in Qur'an 6:86 and 38:48 as the name of a prophet; the verses do not gloss its etymology.
names.meaning_explanation: The name is attested directly in the Qur'an (6:86 and 38:48) as the prophet known in Biblical tradition as Elisha; the deeper etymology belongs to Hebrew (Ĕlîšāʿ) and is not derived from Arabic roots.

names.morphology: Diminutive ʿubayd ('little servant') plus Allah, built on the well-attested Arabic servant-of-God naming pattern that produced names such as Abdullah.
names.primary_meaning: Ubaydullah (ʿubayd Allāh) is an Arabic male name meaning 'little servant of Allah', the diminutive counterpart within the servant-of-God naming pattern that includes Abdullah; the directories disagree on whether the pattern's origin label is Arabic or Urdu, and the lexical analysis here follows Arabic morphology.
names.literal_meaning: The compound joins the diminutive of ʿabd ('servant') with Allah; no Qur'anic verse uses the compound, and the record asserts none.
names.meaning_explanation: The gloss follows the documented directory entries ('Slave of Allah', 'Little Servant'); the record notes that the pattern is a naming convention rather than a Qur'anic word and that no specific historical bearer is asserted.

quranic.note: The ʿabd/ʿubayd-Allah compound is a naming pattern, not a Qur'anic word; no direct verse occurrence is asserted.

names.religious_status: A devotional servant-of-God name; not a prescribed religious formula.
names.religious_explanation: Servant-of-God names are well established in Muslim tradition; this record asserts no ruling about the name and no special virtue attached to it.
names.cultural_note: Recorded as a masculine given name especially in South Asian and Arab Muslim communities; this does not establish a single worldwide frequency.
names.cultural_interpretation: Families may value the devotional sense, but that is a naming preference rather than a prediction about the bearer.
cultural_transmission: Muslim naming communities in South Asia
names.usage_note: A site-internal directory ranking is the only collected metric; the Obaidullah spelling has its own, lower directory rank.

names.name: Wissam
names.morphology: Established Arabic noun (wisām, 'medal, badge, mark of honor') from the w-s-m root ('to mark, stamp'); used as a given name for both men and women in Arabic-speaking communities.
names.short_meaning: Medal, badge, decoration; a mark of honor.
names.primary_meaning: Wissam (wisām) is an Arabic name from the noun wisām, 'medal or badge of honor', itself from the w-s-m root of marking; U.S. data classifies the spelling Wissam for boys while the name is also documented for women, so no single-gender claim is made.
names.literal_meaning: The noun وسام is standard Arabic for a medal or decoration; the record asserts no Qur'anic occurrence for the word.
names.meaning_explanation: The gloss follows the standard Arabic lexical sense of the noun; the record notes the gender disagreement across sources instead of picking one silently.

quranic.note: No Qur'anic occurrence is asserted for the word وسام or its root's name form.

names.religious_status: A lexical name; not a prescribed religious formula.
names.religious_explanation: A positive Arabic lexical name is compatible with Muslim naming traditions, but linguistic origin and a positive meaning are not a religious recommendation or ruling.
names.cultural_note: Recorded as a given name for boys in U.S. data and for both men and women in Arabic-speaking communities; no population-level gender split is asserted.
names.cultural_interpretation: Families may value the honor sense, but that is a naming preference rather than a prediction about the bearer.
names.usage_note: U.S. SSA-derived data exists in scattered years (2017 and 2022); usage is otherwise broader in Arabic-speaking countries.
